C

background.definition: Erectile dysfunction (ED), the more precise and accepted term for impotence, is described as "the inability to achieve or maintain an erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual performance."

list.listitem: The overall incidence of ED in men between the ages of 40 and 70 years is approximately 26 per 1000 person-years. The incidence increases with age.
The average incidence of ED in adult men with type 2 diabetes is approximately 170 per 1000 person-years.
The overall prevalence of ED varies widely depending on the population and how it is assessed. ED occurs in 15% to 50% of adult men.
ED is present in approximately 75% of US men with diabetes mellitus.
Retail pharmacy costs of sildenafil, tadalafil, and vardenafil (Levitra) totaled $1.4 billion in 2006.
The causes of ED are organic (vascular, neurogenic, hormonal, anatomic, or drug induced), psychogenic, or a combination of both.
Organic causes are present in most patients; reduced blood flow to the penis and regional nerve damage are the most common physical causes. Organic causes of ED can be congenital.
Among men with ED, approximately 5%—but as many as 25%—are hypogonadal.
Psychogenic causes of ED can be either generalized or situational. Psychological causes include depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, and conflict with the man's partner.
Erectile dysfunction is a common complication following prostatectomy, whether minimally invasive or open radical surgery is chosen. In fact, ED is more common with the minimally invasive procedure.

A normal erectile response is a complex interaction between vascular and neurologic events initiated by parasympathetic and sympathetic neuronal actions that integrate physiologic stimuli of the penis with sexual perception and desire.

Smooth muscle relaxation, arterial dilatation, and corporovenous compression must all occur simultaneously to achieve an adequate and mutually satisfying erection. A deficiency in any of these elements may lead to ED.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: History of pelvic irradiation or surgery
Hormonal disorders (eg, hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, and hyperprolactinemia)
Illicit drugs (eg, long-term use of alcohol, cocaine, and opiates may all contribute to ED)
Medications (eg, beta-blockers, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, anxiolytics, and antihistamines)
Neurologic conditions (eg, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson disease, stroke, Alzheimer disease, paraplegia, and quadriplegia)
Psychological conditions (eg, depression, guilt, worrying, stress, anxiety, and history of sexual abuse)

list.listitem: Screening for ED is not currently recommended by United States Preventive Services Task Force or other groups. C

A consensus guideline recommends screening for cardiovascular risk factors in men diagnosed with ED but outcome studies are lacking. However, a retrospective cohort study found that after adjusting for age and other cardiovascular risk factors, ED was not an independent risk factor for heart disease. C
There is no recommended diagnostic testing to serve as a gold standard for ED; history and physical examination are sufficient in making an accurate diagnosis in the majority of cases. C

The AUA and WHO recommend limited diagnostic testing in men with ED, including a fasting glucose or HBA1C and lipid profile and evaluation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis with a TSH and total testosterone assay. C
Patients with ED should give a comprehensive sexual history and undergo a focused physical examination.

The sexual history should include erectile insufficiency (onset, duration, progression, severity, nocturnal, self-stimulatory, and visual erotic-induced erections), altered sexual desire, ejaculation, orgasm, sexually induced genital pain, partner sexual function, lifestyle factors, smoking, chronic medical illnesses, pelvic/perineal/penile trauma and surgery, medications, recreational drug use, pelvic radiotherapy, neurologic disease, endocrine disease, psychiatric illness, current psychological state, and depression.

The focused physical examination should include blood pressure and heart rate; body habitus; cardiovascular, neurologic, and genitourinary systems, including penile, testicular, and rectal examination.
The International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF-5), a 5-item questionnaire can be used to determine severity and to monitor response to treatment (see ).
See for an overall approach to diagnostic testing.
The WHO recommends a fasting glucose or HBA1C and lipid profile and evaluation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis with a TSH and total testosterone assay.
The American Urology Association guidelines (2018) recommend a morning serum total testosterone level.
The WHO lists as optional tests: psychological and/or psychiatric consultation, serum prolactin, luteinizing hormone, complete blood count, and urinalysis.

Finally, several specialized evaluations and tests mentioned by the WHO include in-depth psychosexual and relationship evaluation, psychiatric evaluation, nocturnal penile tumescence and rigidity assessment, vascular diagnostics (penile pharmacocavernosometry and pharmacocavernosography, penile arteriography, computed tomography/magnetic resonance imaging, nuclear imaging), specialized endocrine testing (thyroid function studies, hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal function studies, magnetic resonance imaging of the sella turcica), and neurophysiologic testing (vibrometry, bulbocavernosus reflex latency, cavernosal electromyogram, somatosensory evoked potential testing, pudendal and sphincter electromyogram).
Doppler ultrasound is not useful as a diagnostic test for ED.
See the algorithm in for a suggested approach to evaluation of the patient presenting with ED.
First-line therapy for ED should consist of lifestyle modification, drug therapy modification, psychosocial counseling, and oral therapy with phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitors. C

The PDE5 inhibitors are the most effective drugs in the treatment of ED, including ED associated with diabetes and spinal cord injury, and in men with sexual dysfunction secondary to antidepressants. A
Behavioral therapy, either group or individual, plus sildenafil improves sexual functioning and ED better than sildenafil alone. B
Testosterone replacement has little to no effect on erectile function, sexual quality of life, or cardiovascular mortality in the short term. A

Three PDE5 inhibitors—sildenafil, tadalafil, and vardenafil—are currently licensed for the treatment of ED. All are effective, but sildenafil has been the most widely studied. They are considered first-line medical therapy by AUA 2018 guidelines.

Sildenafil has a 30- to 60-minute onset of action and lasts up to 4 hours; vardenafil works within 25 minutes and lasts up to 4 hours; and tadalafil's onset of action is between 16 and 45 minutes and can last up to 36 hours.

Several randomized controlled trials have shown that sildenafil is effective in treating ED, including ED associated with diabetes, spinal cord injury, and antidepressant-associated sexual dysfunction. Compared with placebo, sildenafil improves erections (74% vs 21%; number needed to treat [NNT] = 2) and results in more frequent successful intercourse attempts (57% vs 21%; NNT = 3).

Additionally, three separate Cochrane reviews found some (limited) evidence supporting the efficacy of sildenafil for ED in patients with multiple sclerosis, chronic kidney diseaes (CKD), and antipsychotic-associated sexual dysfunction. However, for patients with COPD, there is insufficient evidence for effective and safe interventions for sexual dysfunction.

A few small flawed studies have compared sildenafil with tadalafil or vardenafil. Patients appear to prefer tadalafil or vardenafil over sildenafil. The largest comparative study to date, a randomized crossover trial, found no meaningful difference in the efficacy between sildenafil and vardenafil.
Tadalafil given daily in a dose of 5 mg is also effective, with clinically significant improvements in sexual quality of life compared with placebo.

In men with hypogonadism, oral testosterone supplementation raises testosterone levels and improves erectile function, although most of the studies are of limited quality and the magnitude of clinical response difficult to determine. Testosterone supplementation in addition to sildenafil was not more effective than sildenafil alone in one study.

After 4 weeks of therapy, men with hypogonadism, defined as a morning serum total testosterone level of less than 400 ng/dL, who fail to respond to sildenafil have significant improvements in erectile function scores if 1% testosterone gel is applied daily in addition to the sildenafil. See chapter on hypogonadism for specific therapy and monitoring of men with ED who are treated with testosterone.

However, a Cochrane review concluded, based on moderate certainty evidence, that testosterone replacement likely has little to no effect on erectile function, sexual quality of life, or cardiovascular mortality compared to placebo in the short term. It appears comparable to placebo in terms of treatment withdrawal due to side effects, prostate-related events, or lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS). Long term, there is considerable uncertainty in the efficacy or safety of testosterone replacement.

PDE5 inhibitors are effective for ED that follows surgery for prostate cancer. However, scheduled PDE5 use ("penile rehabilitation") post-radical prostatectomy does not appear to improve ED outcomes more than on-demand use.
Recreational use of PDE5 inhibitors is common among younger adults without ED, 21% in one population-based survey, half of whom had combined it with alcohol or drugs.

Consider intracavernous alprostadil in men who fail other first-line treatments (see ). A randomized crossover trial found that intracavernous alprostadil was more efficacious, better tolerated, and preferred by men over transurethral alprostadil.
Vacuum constriction devices are a low-cost and noninvasive second-line treatment option for ED, or for those men who cannot tolerate PDE5 inhibitors.

In patients with pharmacotherapy-refractory ED, inflatable penile prostheses may be surgically implanted when medical options have failed. A significant amount of patient education is required to discuss the risks and benefits of this procedure.

Currently, the AUA does not endorse penile venous reconstructive surgery or surgeries to limit venous outflow of the penis; penile arterial reconstructive surgery remains controversial and larger studies are needed to prove efficacy.

Some dietary supplements marketed for the treatment of ED (eg, Super-X and Stamina-RX) contain PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil 30 mg and tadalafil 20 mg, respectively). Although many of these products claim to be free of adverse effects, they may be potentially fatal to patients concomitantly using nitrates.

Korean red ginseng (panax ginseng), dosed 3 times daily, may be an option for treating ED. In one crossover trial, men reported improved erections, but their overall sexual experience was not improved. A Cochrane review, based on low certainty evidence, found ginseng to have trivial effects on ED and negligible rates of adverse events compared to placebo, but no studies evaluated ginseng against more proven therapies like PDE5 inhibitors.
A meta-analysis found that oral yohimbine was superior to placebo for the effective treatment of ED (NNT = 4; 95% CI, 2-8) and side effects were limited and manageable.
When there is no definable medical etiology for a man's ED and a psychological cause is suspected, behavioral therapy and/or removal of the negative psychosocial factor may be beneficial.

A Cochrane review found that men who were randomized to receive group therapy plus sildenafil showed significant improvement in successful intercourse and were less likely to drop out of the study than those receiving sildenafil alone. Group psychotherapy plus sildenafil also significantly improved symptoms of ED compared with sildenafil alone.
No differences were found regarding the effectiveness of psychosocial interventions for the treatment of ED compared with local injection, vacuum devices, and other psychosocial techniques.
Education, physician support, and reassurance may be sufficient to restore acceptable sexual function in some men with ED.

After 2 years of follow-up, obese men with ED receiving detailed advice on how to lose at least 10% of their body mass through lifestyle modification had improvement in their IIEF-5 scores, while men who were only given general information about lifestyle changes had no improvement.

Two studies compared continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) with sildenafil for patients with obstructive sleep apnea and ED; sildenafil was more effective. Similarly, a Cochrane review found low certainty evidence for the efficacy of sildenafil over CPAP for men with ED over a 12 week period.
One RCT found that in men suffering from ED with Peyroine's disease, penile traction therapy utilizing the RestoreX therapy device resulted in clinically meaningful improvements in erectile function.

AUA guidelines do not find evidence to support use of stem cell therapy, platelet rich plasma therapy, or extracorporeal shock wave therapy. Additionally, a Cochrane review found small, clinically insignificant effect on erectile dysfunction for low-intensity shockwave therapy in the short term.
Eroxon®, was approved by the FDA on June 9, 2023 as an over-the-counter (OTC) non-medicated topical formulation for treatment of erectile dysfunction.

One systematic review and meta analysis found that combination therapy for erectile dysfunction—most often PDE5 inhibitors combined with agents like testosterone, antioxidants, vacuum devices, or shockwave therapy—was found to be more effective than monotherapy, without increasing adverse events. The greatest benefits were seen in men with difficult-to-treat ED, hypogonadism, or post-prostatectomy, though some combinations were supported by only single studies.
Duration of therapy is most commonly lifelong because most patients will require some form of pharmacotherapy and/or behavioral therapy for life once the condition begins.
Weight loss and increased physical activity may improve ED; these recommendations also serve as powerful motivators for men to make lifestyle changes that minimize cardiovascular risk.
Most cases of ED can be appropriately managed by primary care physicians via a thorough evaluation and an empiric trial with a PDE5 inhibitor.
Referral to a urologist is indicated when empiric therapy with PDE5 inhibitors is not satisfactory, and for discussion of other treatment modalities described above.
Referral to a behavioral psychotherapist is indicated when the patient and/or the patient and his partner feel that this may be beneficial.

Patients taking PDE5 inhibitors should not take nitrates concomitantly. Although no safe dosing interval has been determined between these classes, it is suggested that a 24-hour interval be used for sildenafil and a 48-hour interval be used for tadalafil.

In men with known coronary artery disease undergoing stress testing, sildenafil does not affect symptoms, exercise duration, or exercise-induced cardiac ischemia. Significant cardiac events reported to be associated with sildenafil use are more likely to be related to the sexual activity rather than the direct use of the drug.
summarizes recommendations for the evaluation of patients with coronary artery disease prior to a return to sexual activity.

The various ED treatments cause a wide spectrum of side effects: PDE5 inhibitors may cause headache, facial flushing, indigestion, and nasal congestion; intraurethral alprostadil may cause local penile pain, urethral bleeding, dizziness, and urinary tract infection symptoms; and intracorporal injection with alprostadil may cause priapism, penile pain, penile hematoma, penile edema, and palpable nodules or plaques.
PDE5 inhibitors are metabolized by the liver, and the dosage should be adjusted for patients with hepatic impairment.
Oral terbutaline (5 mg) is better than placebo in causing detumescence (42% vs 15%) in patients with medication-induced priapism.
Most cases of ED are correctable with a combination of pharmacotherapy, appropriate sexual arousal, and psychotherapy, if indicated. C
The IIEF-5 can be used to monitor response to treatment (see ). B

In elderly men with slight or no signs of vascular disease, erectile function scores improved and there was an increase in nocturnal erections 1 month after competing 3 months of alternate-day tadalafil, while there was no improvement in control patients.
Those with ED have a higher risk of having osteoporosis and therefore bone mineral density testing should be considered. Conversely, those with osteoporosis should be assessed for ED.

cell.label: Obtain a comprehensive sexual history, risk factor analysis, and vital signs, and perform a detailed cardiovascular, neurologic, and genitourinary physical examination.
Complete IIEF-5 questionnaire to categorize erectile dysfunction severity.

Obtain a fasting serum glucose or glycosylated hemoglobin and fasting lipid profile.Optional studies include thyroid-stimulating hormone, total testosterone, and prolactin. Definable medical etiology?
Maximize treatment of coronary heart disease, diabetes, lipids, hypertension, hypogonadism, hypothyroidism, obesity, and metabolic syndrome.

First-line therapy: (1) lifestyle and drug therapy modification (avoid antihistamines, beta-blockers, benzodiazepines, serotonin-specific reuptake inhibitors); (2) oral therapy with PDE5 inhibitors (must ensure patient is not taking nitrates); and (3) androgen replacement therapy, if patient has clinical hypogonadism.
Second-line therapy: (1) intraurethral or intracavernous alprostadil, or (2) vacuum pump therapy.
Consider referral to urology for an implantable pump device if other methods fail. Consider screening for undetected cardiovascular disease.

Consider: screen for psychological disorder (eg, anxiety, bipolar disorder, depression) or substance abuse; referral for behavioral therapy, either individual or with partner; removal of negative psychosocial factor.

feature.caption: Recommendations of the Second Princeton Consensus Conference Regarding Sexual Activity and Treatment of Erectile Dysfunction.

list.listitem: Asymptomatic with fewer than 3 major cardiovascular risk factors (excluding male gender)
Controlled hypertension
Mild, stable angina pectoris
Postrevascularization with no residual ischemia
History of myocardial infarction (6-8 weeks prior)
Mild valvular disease
Left ventricular dysfunction (New York Heart Association [NYHA] Class I)
Other cardiovascular conditions (including pericarditis, mitral valve prolapse, atrial fibrillation with controlled ventricular response)

tr.td: No special testing or evaluation indicated prior to resumption of sexual activity or initiation of erectile dysfunction therapy

list.listitem: Asymptomatic with 3 or more major cardiovascular risk factors (excluding male gender)
Moderate, stable angina pectoris
History of myocardial infarction (2-6 weeks prior)
Left ventricular dysfunction (NYHA Class II)
Noncardiac sequelae of atherosclerotic disease

tr.td: Further testing or evaluation (to classify patient at either high or low risk) indicated before resumption of sexual activity

list.listitem: Unstable or refractory angina pectoris
Uncontrolled hypertension
Congestive heart failure (NYHA Class III or IV)
Recent myocardial infarction (less than 2 weeks prior)
Malignant arrhythmias
Left ventricular dysfunction
Obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

tr.td: Deferment of sexual activity indicated until cardiovascular condition has stabilized or cardiovascular specialist has issued clearance to resume sexual activity

feature.caption: International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF-5) Questionnaire.

tr.td: 1. How do you rate your confidence that you could get and keep an erection?
2. When you had erections with sexual stimulation, how often were your erections hard enough for penetration?
3. During sexual intercourse, how often were you able to maintain your erection after you had penetrated (entered) your partner?
4. During sexual intercourse, how difficult was it to maintain your erection to completion of intercourse?
5. When you attempted sexual intercourse, how often was it satisfactory for you?
